title: Your Fridge Doesn't Make Cold, It Moves Heat Into Your Kitchen
fb_caption: Your fridge doesn't really make cold. Inside, a liquid refrigerant runs through thin tubes and evaporates, soaking up heat from your food. A compressor squeezes that gas until it's hotter than your kitchen, and the coils on the back or underneath release the heat into the room. That's why an open fridge door won't cool the room: the fridge just runs harder and your kitchen ends up warmer. Be honest: how long do you stand at the open fridge hunting for a snack?
engagement_comment: Be honest: how long do you stand at the open fridge hunting for a snack? 1 = in and out in seconds, 2 = a good minute, 3 = until someone tells me to close it.
sources: Danfoss, How a refrigerator works - basic training (refrigerant evaporates in the evaporator and absorbs heat from inside; the compressor raises pressure and temperature; the condenser releases the heat outside the cabinet): https://www.danfoss.com/en-us/service-and-support/fix-and-troubleshooting/air-condition-and-refrigeration-installer-hub/the-fridge-how-it-works/

Sears Home Services, How Does a Refrigerator Work? (compressor makes the refrigerant hotter than the room air; condenser coils on the back or underneath release the heat and the refrigerant turns back into a liquid; evaporator absorbs heat inside): https://www.searshomeservices.com/blog/how-does-a-refrigerator-work
iFixit, How Does a Refrigerator Work? (vapor-compression cycle: evaporator, compressor, condenser coils, expansion device): https://www.ifixit.com/Wiki/How_a_Refrigerator_Works

University of Illinois Physics Van, Open Refrigerator (the fridge is a heat pump; with the door open it runs more and puts more heat into the room than it removes, so the room's average temperature rises): https://van.physics.illinois.edu/ask/listing/1790

beats.text: Your fridge doesn't really make cold. It moves heat out of your food and into your kitchen.
Inside, a liquid refrigerant runs through thin tubes and evaporates, soaking up heat from your food.
Then a compressor near the bottom squeezes that gas, which makes it hot, hotter than your kitchen.
Coils on the back or underneath release that heat into your kitchen, and the refrigerant turns liquid again.
Here's the twist. An open fridge door won't cool the room. The fridge runs harder, and your kitchen gets warmer.
